A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 43 pages of v2 and 51 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, algorithms, and Figure 1, support comparison. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figure 1 report original numerical experiments comparing three denoisers and examining samples generated by the learned GNN.

after.justification: Section 6 and Figure 1 retain the original denoising and sampling results, with training details provided in Appendix X.

M1.justification: The explicit submatrix algorithms, GNN architecture, and Euler sampler are retained. Appendix D adds an adaptation that modifies arbitrary near-optimal denoisers in the very sparse regime through a detection gate constructed using Gaussian splitting and thresholded spectral estimation. This extends the existing drift-modification procedure.

E1.justification: The empirical coverage remains denoising and sampling synthetic sparse rank-one matrices, with n = 350 and k = 20. V3's tensor, coding, posterior-sampling, and constraint-satisfaction examples are theoretical applications or future directions, not additional evaluated datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: The numerical comparison retains the spectral-plus-projection denoiser, its 25-step power-iteration approximation, and the learned GNN. The spectral algorithm changes from Algorithm 1 in v2 to Algorithm 2 in v3 through renumbering, not comparator replacement.

E3.justification: The reported GNN training sample count changes from 10,000 in v2 Section 6 to 30,000 in v3 Appendix X; the associated percentage changes from approximately 1% to 3%. The 15,000-sample evaluation set, matrix dimensions, architecture, and training curriculum remain unchanged. This establishes a reported setting revision, not that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Both versions retain the same MSE-versus-noise illustration, generated-sample norm histogram, and qualitative observations about network initialization and progressive-depth training. No new empirical ablations, robustness tests, or supplementary case studies are reported.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent training-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the numerical illustration. Changes to theoretical probability bounds are mathematical revisions, not changes in empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figure 1 retains identical plotted content. Both versions report that the GNN outperforms the spectral comparators, fails to overcome the algorithmic barrier, and generates samples near zero, with a Wasserstein lower bound of 0.48 versus the theoretical 0.50. The revised training count does not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: V3 introduces distribution-general Theorems 1 and 3, explicit detection and pure-noise assumptions, the very-sparse Corollary D.1, and new derivations and proofs in Appendices B, C, G, and V. The matrix-specific results are retained as applications. V2 Theorem 6 becomes Corollary 5.1 with revised assumptions, a corrected high-SNR inequality, and a shorter guarantee: C0 n with bounded step size replaces n^(1+gamma0) with arbitrary positive step size. Appendix K also revises the very-sparse concentration argument.

C1.justification: The abstract's central negative claim is retained, but the introduction and contribution summary now foreground two general impossibility results for distributions satisfying specified assumptions. Sparse matrices become an application rather than the principal scope of the formal claims. The all-Lipschitz claim also explicitly requires suitable behavior on pure noise.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantial explanations linking estimator shrinkage, efficient detection, and sampling failure. Section 5 explains why the mixture distribution enforces small outputs on pure noise. Section 3.2.2 and Appendix B expand applicability discussions, including time reparameterization and applications requiring further work. Section 3.1 explicitly distinguishes its assumptions from the usual information-computation-gap definition and leaves their formal relationship for future work.

D1.justification: The reproducibility description revises the required training data from 10,000 to 30,000 samples. The GNN architecture, power-method initialization, time-sampling probabilities, progressive-depth training, and evaluation sample count are otherwise retained in Appendix X. Their relocation does not constitute newly disclosed implementation detail.

R1.justification: V3 adds six references supporting connections to time-reversed diffusions, tensor PCA, coding theory, and Bayesian matrix estimation. These include Song et al. (2021), Haussmann and Pardoux (1986), and Montanari and Richard (2014). The existing diffusion-sampling and computational-hardness literature remains central; the added positioning is a limited extension.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution summary are substantially rewritten, and Section 3 is reorganized around general assumptions and a theorem followed by applications. Concrete denoisers and their statements move to Appendix E, detailed reduction statements to Appendix S, and numerical implementation details to Appendix X. This substantially changes the narrative and main-text/appendix organization.

P2.justification: Figure 1 retains its panels, axes, and plotted content but moves from page 12 to page 13. The two algorithm boxes move into Appendix E and exchange numbers. The basic visual format remains stable. The retained figure legend still references spectral Algorithm 1, although the corresponding algorithm is now Algorithm 2.

improvement.justification: V3 provides a clearer general framework and corrects v2's overlapping low- and high-SNR conditions, while revising assumptions and shortening the Lipschitz failure horizon. However, the new Appendix V proof bounds KL between the ideal and implemented processes using only the squared estimated drift, although Eq. (1) gives the ideal process its own drift. This leaves a consequential step supporting the new general Theorem 3 unjustified as written. The explanatory gains and unresolved mathematical support prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
